New open model sets a record on reasoning benchmarks

A research lab released an open-weight language model on Thursday that it says outperforms every other publicly available model on a range of mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks. The model, which has roughly seventy billion parameters, can be downloaded and run on a single high-end server, according to the announcement.

The lab said the improvements came mostly from better training data rather than a larger architecture. Engineers filtered several trillion tokens of web text, kept only documents that passed a series of quality checks, and added a large set of synthetic problems with verified step-by-step solutions. The final training run took about six weeks.

Independent researchers who tested the model ahead of the release said the results looked consistent with the published numbers, although they cautioned that benchmark scores do not always translate into better performance in everyday tasks. Several noted that the model still makes arithmetic mistakes on long problems and sometimes states wrong answers with confidence.

The release comes amid a broader debate over whether powerful models should be published openly. Supporters argue that open weights let universities and small companies study and improve the technology, while critics worry that safety measures can be removed once a model is available for anyone to modify. The lab said it ran red-teaming exercises before release.

The company plans to publish a technical report with full details of the training data pipeline next month. It also said a smaller version, designed to run on laptops, is in development and could be released before the end of the year if internal evaluations go well. Pricing for a hosted version of the model has not been announced yet.
